[[Image:BoysSurfaceTopView.PNG|thumb|Boy's surface from near the top ([[Robert Bryant (mathematician)|R. Bryant's]] parameterization)]]
'''Werner Boy''' ({{IPA|de|ˈvɛɹnɐ bɔɪ|lang}}; 4 May 1879 − 6 September 1914) was a German [[mathematician]]. He was the discoverer and [[eponym]] of [[Boy's surface]]—a [[dimension|three-dimensional]] projection of the [[real projective plane]] without [[Mathematical singularity|singularities]], the first of its kind. He discovered it in 1901 after his thesis adviser, [[David Hilbert]], asked him to prove that it was not possible to immerse the real projective plane in three-dimensional space. Boy sketched several models of the surface, and discovered that it could have 3-fold rotational symmetry, but was unable to find a [[parametric equation|parametric model]] for the surface. It was not until 1978 that [[Bernard Morin]] found the first parametrisation, with the [[Computer-assisted proof|aid of computers]].<ref>{{citation
 | last = Morin | first = Bernard
 | issue = 13
 | journal = Comptes Rendus Hebdomadaires des Séances de l'Académie des Sciences
 | mr = 551770
 | pages = A879–A882
 | title = Équations du retournement de la sphère
 | volume = 287
 | year = 1978}}</ref><ref>{{citation
 | last = Apéry | first = François
 | doi = 10.1007/978-3-322-89569-1
 | isbn = 9783322895691
 | page = 54
 | publisher = Vieweg+Teubner Verlag
 | title = Models of the Real Projective Plane
 | year = 1987| doi-access = free
 }}</ref>

After completing his dissertation, Boy worked as a high school teacher in [[Krefeld, Germany]]. He later returned to his birth town of Barmen (today [[Wuppertal]]) to teach. He died as a soldier in the first weeks of [[World War I]] on 6 September 1914.
